China's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, supported by an AI-driven electronics boom and higher energy prices, while consumer-facing industries squeezed by weak demand continued to be a drag.
Profits at sizeable industrial firms surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, having risen 15.5% through September.
That extends a notable rebound in 2026 after three years of declines followed by a tepid 0.6% growth last year, with profits on track to log their strongest annual expansion since 2021.
Despite the sharp headline figure, "the recovery has yet to broaden into a more durable improvement in corporate profitability," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, as the rebound was largely led by upstream sectors amid higher energy prices.
China's economy has been running at two speeds, with AI-related manufacturing and exports powering growth while household consumption has been lagging. Retail sales grew a smaller-than-expected 0.4% in October, and fixed-asset investment steepened declines to 8.1% in the first 10 months.
Profit gains were concentrated in a set of sectors tied to the global AI buildout and higher commodity prices, while consumer-facing manufacturers struggled to pass on higher input costs, squeezing margins.
Earnings in the electronics sector doubled in the first 10 months from the same period last year, as demand for AI computing power lifted memory chips and related manufacturing, said Yu Weining, chief statistician of the NBS.
Profits in high-tech manufacturing jumped 50.9%, outpacing the industry as a whole, Yu added. Makers of spacecraft and launch vehicles reported a 63.2% rise.
Commodity producers also saw sharp growth in profits as demand tied to renewable energy and AI pushed up copper and aluminum prices, Yu said. Petroleum processors swung to a combined profit from a loss a year earlier.
Showcasing an increasingly bifurcated economy, industries tied to consumers and construction recorded steepening losses. Automakers saw profits drop 26% in the first 10 months, wider than the previous month, as costs outpaced a modest revenue increase.
Producers of construction materials such as cement and glass, and furniture makers continued to suffer the fallout from a prolonged real estate slump, with profits falling 46.7% and 52.4%, respectively.
Accounts receivable, or money owed to businesses by their customers, and finished-goods inventories also grew faster than revenue, official data showed, underscoring the strain on companies across sectors.
Fiscal boost
Overall activity in October picked up "substantially" compared to the past couple of months, expanding 2.4% from a year earlier, according to Capital Economics' China Activity Proxy, a gauge that excludes official data in favor of low-profile indicators, such as freight and port traffic, that are "less politically-sensitive and so less likely to be manipulated."
The growth in October was led by strong external demand and exports, even as manufacturing activity for domestic goods languished, said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics.
Local governments stepped up fiscal spending for the first time since February last month, Fahy said, but that "had little impact" on arresting the property slump and reviving domestic demand.

They’ve rolled up the red carpet, opened all the envelopes and thanked the engraving artists for their services. But just because all the MLB Awards have been handed out for 2026 doesn’t mean we can’t still salute some superlative seasons.
What follows is our annual list of award-worthy players who did not receive any major hardware -- the BBWAA’s MVP, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year or Reliever of the Year honors; the All-MLB First and Second Team selections; the Clemente Award; the Aaron Awards; the Silver Slugger Awards; the Gold Glove Awards; the Outstanding DH Award; the Comeback Player of the Year Award; the other Reliever of the Year Awards; and the postseason awards.
Oh, and none of these guys was Manager or Executive of the Year, either. Rude.
Presenting the 2026 All-Awardless Team. The discarded envelopes, please!
Catcher: Drake Baldwin, Braves
We had an unusually deep cast of award-worthy catchers this year. Liam Hicks provided big value for the state of Florida with the Marlins and then the Rays, Carter Jensen looked like a keeper for Kansas City, Hunter Goodman belted 41 bombs for the Rockies and Shea Langeliers exceeded 20 homers and 20 doubles for the A’s for the second straight year.
But our imaginary award goes to Baldwin, the 2025 NL Rookie of the Year who maintained a major role on the division-winning Braves in his sophomore season. He slashed .284/.358/.459 with 25 homers and 21 doubles, and his 3.9 bWAR trailed only Silver Slugger and Gold Glove winners Gabriel Moreno (Diamondbacks) and Dillon Dingler (Tigers).
First base: Rafael Devers, Giants
The 2026 Giants were a hot mess despite getting the kind of production expected of Devers when he was acquired in a mid-2025 blockbuster. His 37 homers were his most since 2021, and the most by a Giants player since Barry Bonds hit 45 in 2004. His 36 doubles were his most since 2022. He slashed .258/.340/.525 with a 142 OPS+ (42% better than league average) that ranked third among qualified first basemen, behind All-MLB Team members Willson Contreras (153) and Pete Alonso (149).
Devers’ .988 OPS after the All-Star break was the fourth-best in MLB among those with at least 200 plate appearances. It was a little surprising that he didn’t get any down-ballot MVP support, though the Giants’ competitive standing likely played into that.
Second base: JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals
You could (metaphorically) feel Wetherholt’s pain when he spent 17 days on the injured list late in the season with a wrist issue, because that injury cost him what was a pretty decent shot at the NL Rookie of the Year honor (he wound up finishing third).
Wetherholt couldn’t match Reds first baseman Sal Stewart’s offensive production. But his 17 homers, 15 doubles and 14 steals paired with his elite defensive to make this 2024 first-rounder an impact player. With elite range up the middle, Wetherholt’s 25 Outs Above Average ranked behind only NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong (26) in all of MLB.
Shortstop: Otto Lopez, Marlins
Though he fell short of award acclaim, the 27-year-old Lopez was one of the biggest breakthrough stories in MLB this season. He made a 114-point leap in OPS with a .786 mark, finished fifth among qualifiers with a .305 average and led the Majors with 191 hits. Lopez was in the top 20 in the Majors with 32 doubles and top three with nine triples.

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs initiated coverage of Andritz AG (LON:0MJZ) with a "buy" rating, arguing that the Austrian industrial equipment maker is entering a new phase of earnings growth as its expanding hydropower backlog converts into more profitable projects.
The investment bank set a 12-month price target of €95, compared with its reference price of €75.90, implying potential upside of 25.2%.
It said improving visibility over project execution, stronger contract pricing and a favourable business mix should support earnings growth even without a broad recovery across industrial end-markets.
Hydropower is central to the investment case. Goldman expects revenue from the division to increase to €2.7 billion by 2028 from €1.7 billion in 2025, while comparable operating profit before amortisation (EBITA) more than doubles to €247 million from €118 million. Margins are forecast to expand to 9.1% from 6.8% over the same period.
The improvement reflects a shift in the nature of Andritz's project portfolio. Earlier hydropower contracts were often secured at tight fixed prices, leaving the company exposed to increases in input costs during delivery.
Newer orders offer better pricing and stronger contractual protections, allowing more cost increases to be passed on to customers.
Goldman expects these contracts to progressively replace lower-margin legacy projects, improving profitability as the enlarged backlog is executed. Investment in pumped-storage facilities, refurbishment of ageing hydropower plants and grid-stability equipment should provide additional demand.
The bank expects hydropower to account for 53% of Andritz's forecast group comparable EBITA growth between 2025 and 2028.
Goldman forecasts group revenue rising to €9.6 billion in 2028 from €7.9 billion in 2025, with comparable EBITA increasing to €942 million from €698 million.

Gainesville students prepare supplemental food bags for the district’s weekend food program, which serves approximately 200 students each week (Courtesy of Gainesville R-V School District).
GAINESVILLE — An elementary school in rural southern Missouri ranks among the state’s top performers for academic growth in English language arts, an achievement its superintendent credits to improved instruction, dedicated teachers and efforts to address challenges students face outside the classroom.
According to Saint Louis University’s PRiME Center 2026 academic growth report, Gainesville Elementary School ranked 15th among 251 rural elementary schools in Missouri for three-year growth in English language arts, earning a growth score of 89.9. The rankings reflect student performance from the 2022-23 through 2024-25 school years.
The score measures student growth rather than overall proficiency. The report found that 55.1% of Gainesville students tested proficient or advanced in English language arts.
Superintendent Justin Gilmore, now in his seventh year leading the Gainesville R-V School District, said the recognition reflects an approach that places students’ academic, physical and emotional needs at the center of the district’s work.
“We’ve taken a holistic approach,” Gilmore said. “We have to take care of kids’ basic needs before we can ensure they’re ready to learn.”
Located in Ozark County, Gainesville is a community of approximately 700 residents. Gilmore said economic challenges facing local families have influenced the district’s approach to education.
To strengthen instruction, district leaders researched curricula used by high-performing Missouri schools and took teachers to visit those districts to observe classroom practices firsthand.
“We took teachers to visit other districts and see their approaches in action,” Gilmore said. “We have phenomenal teachers, and we trust them to help lead those decisions.”
The district also provided Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading and Spelling (LETRS) training, a professional development program focused on the science of reading, including phonics and foundational literacy skills.

Two things are happening in trail running and ultrarunning at the same time: More athletes are talking openly about anxiety, depression, burnout, and eating disorders. And more are hiring someone to help them race with better focus, confidence, and composure.
Both are great. The trouble is that we’ve started treating them as the same thing, and they aren’t.
Mental health and mental performance overlap, but they call for different kinds of help. When runners can’t tell them apart, they end up in the wrong office. The athlete who needs help with performance skills spends months in talk therapy, or the athlete with depression gets handed a visualization script.
Confusing mental health with mental performance, and vice versa, costs people time, money, and sometimes their well-being. Ultrarunning already has plenty of ways to burn all three without adding this to the pile.
Mental Health Versus Mental Performance
Mental health is about how you function as a person: your mood, anxiety, sleep, relationships, relationship with food and your body, and capacity to get through an ordinary Tuesday. Clinical work here — diagnosing and treating depression, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, trauma, and substance use — belongs to licensed professionals: psychologists, psychiatrists, counselors, and clinical social workers. This is not the realm of your coach, a podcast host, or the person at the aid station with strong opinions about mantras.
Mental performance focuses on how you execute a specific task under specific demands: pacing a 50 miler, staying composed when the weather turns on you, managing your attention at hour nine of an ultra, or bouncing back from a DNF. The work is skills-based and educational. Think of it as strength training for your attention and self-talk, not clinical treatment.
However, the two do share a border. Anxiety management shows up in both, and someone who’s in a good place psychologically may be better positioned to train and race well. But maybe not.
Mental health and performance answer different questions. Mental health asks, “Are you ok?” Mental performance asks, “What do you need to be able to do, and how do we build that skill?”
The sport psychology field has wrestled with this differentiation for years, and the answer keeps coming back the same. The European Federation of Sports Psychology (FEPSAC) position statement on athlete mental health calls for clear models of service provision because the roles between mental health support and mental performance consulting are distinct and the risks of blurring them are real (1). A later international consensus statement made a similar case: Improving athlete mental health takes qualified, coordinated care, not a general-purpose “mindset” approach (2).
Dr. Lara Pence, a licensed clinical psychologist who works with professional and elite athletes, frames the difference as functioning versus performance. Mental health asks, “Am I functioning at a certain level that allows me to show up for myself, in relationships, and in the world?” Performance, she says, “is much more about dialing into a specific aspect, with one’s mind as the priority.”
Emma K. Wagner, a mental performance consultant, puts the performance side in plain terms. On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang had been reinstated, and the shares rose 31.5%.
The episode highlighted a degree of key-person risk that I had underestimated. Nvidia's product cadence and customer confidence have always been closely tied to Huang. His return obviously removes the immediate succession problem. However, it leaves investors with a governance question.
The board reinstated him before completing its independent investigation, shortly after creating a National Security and Export Control Committee on November 17 and alongside launching a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Those oversight steps are the right moves, but they do not excuse reversing a major leadership decision before the facts are settled.
For my Bullish thesis, Huang's return is a stabilizer, though stronger governance is still required.

Nvidia's results still point to very strong AI demand, and that's the part of the argument I find most compelling. Management has guided to around $130 billion in Q4 FY2027 revenue, plus or minus 3%, all the way through the end of the year, despite assuming zero Data Center compute revenue from China.
Nvidia's product roadmap also gives me confidence the company can sustain growth. The company has started shipping Vera Rubin NVL72, with systems already operating at major cloud partners. This comes as some of its biggest customers continue to invest heavily in AI infrastructure. Meta (META), Google (GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN) all raised their capital spending plans during their October earnings updates, suggesting that demand for the computing infrastructure Nvidia provides could remain strong.

What Wells Fargo's New Bond Issuance Signals For Stock Investors
Wells Fargo (WFC) has launched a fresh round of fixed income offerings, including callable senior unsecured notes maturing between 2029 and 2036, alongside a separate zero coupon issue due 2041.
The menu spans fixed coupon securities such as 5.35% notes due December 7, 2029 and 5.50% notes due December 7, 2030, both priced at 100% of face value with modest discounts. There are also 5.65% notes maturing in 2031, plus longer dated paper including 6.00% and 6.20% bonds stretching to 2036 and 2041, as well as 5.85% notes due 2033.
Alongside the new announcements, Wells Fargo recently completed several smaller tranches, ranging from US$195,000 to US$6.303 million in principal, and a larger US$30 million zero coupon Euro MTN due November 18, 2041. Each of these instruments is senior and unsecured, which places them high in the creditor pecking order if something goes wrong, but still behind depositors. It also leaves existing shareholders structurally junior to this new debt.
For you as an equity investor, these bond deals matter less for their ticket sizes and more for what they say about how the bank is funding itself. Issuing callable medium term notes gives Wells Fargo added levers to adjust its liability mix over time, while fixed coupons and specific discounts per security help set a reference point for how the market is currently pricing the group's credit risk.
None of this automatically makes the stock more or less attractive. It does give you another data point to weigh alongside earnings expectations, valuation metrics and recent share performance. Over the past month the stock has slipped 1.7%, and over the past 3 months it has declined about 5.1%, even though the business reports annual revenue of US$83.1b and net income of US$21.98b across its four operating segments.

Saudi Arabia's economic diversification strategy has moved from "spending and delivery at any cost" to "spending and delivery at the right cost," Economy Minister Faisal Alibrahim told CNBC on Friday.
It comes after the Kingdom scaled back or cut several flagship projects as it endures a sharp economic contraction.
Alibrahim also said Saudi Arabia would "stop at nothing from realizing long-term sustainable stability in the region" amid ongoing Houthi strikes on civilian and energy infrastructure that have killed and injured dozens and repeatedly rocked oil markets.
"The phase we're in today is one where every riyal is deployed with greater precision... it was clear that while we want to diversify or restructure our economy to depend less on government spend, there was a lot of catch-up that needed to be done, and for that, you saw government spend leading the way," Alibrahim told CNBC's Dan Murphy.
"Right now, that is shifting from spending and delivery at any cost to spending and delivering at the right cost. We're moving towards a policy-first approach to many of our policy areas and... objectives. We're also creating a clearer business environment, one that aligns the regulatory environment in the Kingdom with international laws."
That includes the recent announcement of a 15% minimum effective tax rate on multinational profits, which Alibrahim said would "create a clearer environment for the private sector to operate," as the government looks to attract more external investment.
Saudi pulls back non-essential spending
Saudi Arabia has been on a mammoth capital spending spree since it launched its Vision 2030 plan to reduce its dependence on oil revenue in 2016, deploying the resources of its sovereign wealth fund — the Public Investment Fund, or PIF.
But more recently, it has reassessed the cost and commercial prospects of initiatives such as the new economic region NEOM and the futuristic "The Line" city, withdrawn funding from the LIV Golf tournament and halted construction on a planned giant skyscraper in Riyadh. In January, it said it would postpone hosting the 2029 Asian Winter Games, which had been scheduled for Trojena, a planned part of NEOM.
Saudi Arabia is meanwhile grappling with the destabilizing effects of ongoing strikes by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, which have hit targets including the PIF tower, Riyadh Airport and the country's largest oil refinery. The danger forced the Kingdom to call off its big international investor conference, dubbed "Davos in the Desert," which was due to be attended by some of the biggest figures in global finance in November.
"The human cost of crisis has been real, and so has been the economic cost," Alibrahim told CNBC.
